questions.prompt: Four builders each begin work, and each quietly picks a different date format because nobody decided one. Their outputs later fail to combine. Where was the missing node?
options: A deliverable node for the combine step
A wayfinding node whose output is the date-format decision and whose consumers are the four builders
A spike that measures how long each builder wants to spend
A soft edge between the builders
questions.explanation: The shared unresolved answer is a decision needed by all four, so it belongs on the graph as one node that gates them. Option A describes the fan-in, which is fine — the failure is upstream of it. Option C confuses a spike (produces knowledge) with the decision that was actually missing. Option D removes an edge the builders do not have; there was no explicit connection at all, which is the problem.

questions.prompt: A team says "we decided to use an event bus months ago" but every new component re-asks and two have since chosen different queues. What is the wayfinding failure?
options: The decision was made but no record was produced, so it cannot be consumed — a decision that lives in conversation blocks invisibly and gets re-litigated
The event bus should have been a spike
The components needed a longer lease
questions.explanation: The output of a wayfinding node is the record; without it, downstream nodes cannot read the commitment and drift. Option A is the tempting reading, but the decision was made — the failure is that its output was never written down. Option C swaps a commitment for knowledge-gathering. Option D is a claiming concept and unrelated.

questions.prompt: A single node needs to know the retention period for logs. Nobody else needs this. Should you add a separate wayfinding node that gates other work?
options: Yes — every decision must be a top-level node
No — make the decision a node that gates only that one consumer, so it does not become a bottleneck for unrelated work
No — leave it out of the graph and let the builder decide
Yes, and make it block the whole frontier so it is resolved first
questions.explanation: A decision node should block exactly its consumers; with one consumer, scoping it narrowly keeps the decision from serialising unrelated work. Option A is the tempting rule-taken-too-far and creates bottlenecks. Option C is the invisible-dependency bug: an unassigned question the builder will guess at. Option D is over-blocking — the retention decision has one consumer and does not belong on the critical path of everything else.

questions.prompt: You cannot phase a blocker as "option A or option B, choose one, here is why" — it is really "go find out whether the vendor API supports webhooks." What kind of node is this, and what comes next?
options: A wayfinding node; write the decision record now
A spike — it produces knowledge; the decision it informs becomes its own node afterwards
A deliverable; ship the support check as a feature
Nothing — unknown blockers cannot be represented on a graph
questions.explanation: An open question that needs investigating is a spike: its output is a fact, which then feeds a decision node. Option A is tempting because both are "up front," but you cannot commit a choice before the fact exists. Option C ships an investigation as if it were a product. Option D is false — spikes are ordinary nodes and belong on the graph.
